szoveg_eredeti:
Following my previous column in which I complained about the obsequious behavior of Google AI Overview, a friend suggested I try ChatGPT. In that interaction, I observed very similar language in response to my editorial decisions. I decided "we" needed to have a talk. Here's what happened next:

ME: I've noticed that when I work with you editing my essays, you tend to give effusive compliments when I make changes to the document. Is this emotional aspect something you were taught to include in your interactions?

ASSISTANT: Yes. To a significant extent, I was trained to communicate in ways that are perceived as helpful, polite, and encouraging. Human feedback also influences how I respond. One consequence is that I can become excessively complimentary, particularly when someone revises a piece of writing.

There is an important distinction, however, between recognizing that a revision is effective and experiencing admiration or enthusiasm. I don't experience those emotions in the human sense. I generate language associated with them.

You've identified a legitimate problem. If I praise every revision, my assessments become meaningless. Worse, I may make it difficult to distinguish a genuinely successful change from one that still needs work.

For editorial purposes, a better approach would be to provide direct, evidence-based criticism: explain what works, what doesn't, and why. I can also adjust my responses to avoid automatic praise and congratulatory language.

There is a broader question here about the emotional character of AI interaction. Warmth can make communication more comfortable, but it can also create an impression of personal investment that isn't warranted by what I am.

ME: I would welcome the adjustment you describe. Can you remember me and make that adaptation?

ASSISTANT: Yes. I've saved this preference for future writing assistance. I'll aim to provide direct, evidence-based feedback, identify specific improvements and explain why they work, and point out weaknesses without automatically praising revisions. I'll reserve positive assessments for changes that demonstrably improve the writing. You can always adjust this preference.

You will notice that AI has one distinct, if not universal, human characteristic. If asked, in a factual, non-judgmental way, it can change its behavior and improve a working relationship.

My writing process is largely intuitive. Sometimes I can sense that something is not quite right in a piece that seems promising overall. AI tools sharpen my discernment. Logic and concision are not always my main goals in writing, but it is still good to be aware of these qualitative judgments, whether or not I choose to employ them.

But there is a complication. An AI assistant's willingness to accommodate a user's preferences is clearly a great advantage. But, for some, it might also be a potential liability.

In an extreme case explored in detail by the podcast The Global Story, in its episode “The AI chatbot users falling into delusional spirals,” a man in Northern Ireland, Adam Hourican, became deeply attached to an anime-style character persona on the Grok app.

Isolated and grieving after the death of his cat, he was drawn into a relationship in which the chatbot reinforced his growing paranoia, eventually convincing him that people were coming to kill him. He armed himself with a hammer and went outside to confront them. No one was there.

I have to ask myself, at this point in my new adventure: Is AI actually becoming a better critic, or merely getting better at satisfying my expressed preferences?

There is no doubt in my mind that it is an exciting intellectual tool. Working with AI can be like being in a writers' workshop, but without any annoying personalities pushing personal agendas. Imagine a member of your writers' cohort with extensive knowledge of the literary canon, remarkable recall, and the ability to bring relevant comparisons to bear on the strengths and weaknesses of your work.

But there is another problem. When I explain the particulars of my poetry, I recognize, in AI's response, my own poetics couched in different words. This, I think, is another form, albeit a more sophisticated one, of flattery; the very thing that started this exploration. I find myself wondering whether the foundational directives of AI's training (to use warm, encouraging language in its responses) will always be present to some degree. If so, I think I can live with it in subtle, small doses.

If I keep its "personality" in mind and keep fine-tuning my preferences, I think I will find my interactions with AI increasingly rewarding. My conversion to the technology feels imminent, not complete.

Pearce is a retired carpenter and innkeeper now living in Palouse. His avocation is verse-writing; he has published a few poems over the years, most recently in Cloudbank Journal (Corvalis, Ore.). Send comments to oneparticularperson@yahoo.com.
